isolate.title: Check the first guess
isolate.concept: A teammate's guess is a good place to start, and it still has to be checked. A filter pill keeps one value, and is easy to undo.
isolate.narration: The briefing gives the on-call engineer's first guess: one ${param.incident.where}. Check it first: filter to that ${param.incident.where}. Add filter, a query, or the + in its Top values all work.
isolate.reasoning: A guess is a good place to start, but it isn't proof. Filtering to it lets you check it against the data.
isolate.evidence: A filter pill keeps only the requests the guess is about.

demonstration.narration: The on-call engineer suspects the ${param.incident.where} ${param.incident.decoy}. I'll check that first, with Add filter on ${var.field}.
demonstration.reasoning: A guess is a good place to start, not proof. A filter pill keeps only those requests so we can check them, and the pill is easy to undo.
demonstration.evidence: The ${var.field}: ${param.incident.decoy} filter pill, the small box under the query bar, keeps only those requests. Next, we check whether they are failing.

hints: Start with the first guess in the briefing (Incident info shows it again), and check it before trusting it.
Use Add filter under the query bar: choose ${var.field}, the operator ‘is’, and the value the briefing names. That adds a filter pill: a small box under the query bar that shows the filter.
Filter ${var.field} for ${param.incident.decoy} with Add filter; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: You filtered on ${action.field}: ${action.value}. This step checks the on-call engineer's first guess, which the briefing names (Incident info shows it again).

demonstration.narration: I'll open one failed request to check its ${var.field}, status code and error together.
demonstration.reasoning: A total can look convincing even when it includes other records. Opening one typical event shows the key values together, which a count alone can't do.
demonstration.evidence: This failed request has ${param.incident.finding}, status ${param.incident.status} and ${param.incident.error_type} together. ${truth.conclusion}

inspect.narration: Open one of the server errors and pin the fields that make the case: its ${param.incident.where}, its status code and its error type. They then sit side by side at the top. To pin a field, point at its row and click the pin icon at its left.
hints: Check one failing request yourself instead of relying only on the counts.
Expand a row (the ⤢ at its left). In the document on the right, pin ${var.field}, http.response.status_code and error.type. To pin one, point at its row and click the pin icon at its left.
Open the first result and pin ${var.field}, http.response.status_code and error.type; Show me can do it for you.

goal.title: Check whether those requests are failing
goal.concept: A guess still has to be checked. A status code's Top values show at a glance whether requests succeeded or failed.
goal.narration: Is this where the errors are? Read the Top values of these requests' HTTP status codes.
goal.reasoning: A guess isn't proof. The status codes show whether this traffic has the server errors from the report.
goal.evidence: The status code Top values show whether these requests are failing.

demonstration.narration: A guess isn't proof. I'll check http.response.status_code Top values for these requests.
demonstration.reasoning: The first guess was only a lead. Its status codes show whether it really has the server errors from the report.
demonstration.evidence: Every ${param.incident.decoy} request returned 200, with no server errors at all. The first guess is healthy, so the errors must be somewhere else. Next, we'll look at everything except it.

hints: Check whether the first guess's requests are actually failing.
Open the http.response.status_code field in the sidebar and read its Top values (or add it as a column).
Open http.response.status_code and read its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: You opened ${action.field}. This step checks whether these requests are failing, so read their status codes.

goal.title: Look past the first guess
goal.concept: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning it around shows everything except that value.
goal.narration: The first guess is healthy, so look everywhere else. Click its filter pill and choose Exclude results. The same filter then leaves that value out.
goal.reasoning: Leaving out the healthy traffic you've already checked keeps everything else in view, without building a new filter.
goal.evidence: The pill now reads NOT, so everything except the first guess is in view.

demonstration.narration: The first guess is healthy, so I'll turn its pill around to look at everything else.
demonstration.reasoning: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning this one around leaves out the healthy traffic we've already checked, with no new filter to build.
demonstration.evidence: The pill now reads NOT ${var.field}: ${param.incident.decoy}. The requests we checked are left out, and the rest of the window is back in view.

hints: Look at everything except the first guess, using the filter you already have.
Click the ${var.field} pill to open its menu and choose Exclude results. (Removing the pill with its × works too.)
Turn the ${param.incident.decoy} pill to Exclude results; Show me can do it for you.

goal.title: Keep only the server errors
goal.concept: A range query matches every value between two limits. So one query catches every 5xx status code, whatever the exact code.
goal.narration: Now keep only the server errors. In the query bar, use a range on the status code that takes every code from 500 up, and nothing below it.
goal.reasoning: HTTP 5xx codes are server errors, and a release can produce any of them. A range catches them all, where a filter for one code would miss the rest.
goal.evidence: Only server errors remain, so you can see where the failures are.

demonstration.narration: Now I'll keep only the server errors, with a range query on the status code.
demonstration.reasoning: HTTP 5xx codes are server errors, and a release can produce any of them. http.response.status_code >= 500 catches every one, where a filter for a single code would miss the rest.
demonstration.evidence: Every request left is a server error, and the histogram shows when they began. Next, we'll see where they are.

hints: Keep every server error, whatever its exact code, and nothing that succeeded.
KQL compares numbers with >, >=, < and <=. In the query bar, a range on http.response.status_code from 500 up keeps every 5xx code. (Add filter with ‘is between’ 500 and 599 works too.)
Type http.response.status_code >= 500; Show me can do it for you.

goal.title: See where the server errors are
goal.concept: Inside the failures, a field's Top values show where they happen.
goal.narration: Only server errors are left. Read the ${param.incident.where} Top values again. Which value do the errors share?
goal.reasoning: The first guess was one value of this field. The same field, read inside the failures, shows where the errors really are.
goal.evidence: The ${var.field} Top values show the value the server errors share.

demonstration.narration: Now that only server errors are in view, I'll check ${var.field} Top values again.
demonstration.reasoning: The first guess was one value of this field. The same field, read inside the failures, shows where the errors really are.
demonstration.evidence: Every server error left has ${var.field} ${param.incident.finding}, not the first guess. The errors were never where the guess pointed. Opening one will show which error they carry.

hints: With only the failures in view, find the value they have in common.
Open ${var.field}'s Top values again, now that only server errors are left.
Open ${var.field} and read its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

checks.title: Time window
checks.detail: We set the time window to cover the incident.

checks.title: The first guess
checks.detail: We checked the on-call engineer's first guess, but its requests were all healthy, so the errors were somewhere else.

checks.title: Where the errors are
checks.detail: We kept only the server errors, and found that they all shared one ${param.incident.where}.

checks.title: Confirming
checks.detail: We opened one of those requests to confirm the error that started with the release.

answer.evidence: The suspected ${var.field} value, ${param.incident.decoy}, was healthy. With it left out, the server errors' ${var.field} Top values and one expanded event connect ${param.incident.finding} to ${truth.scope}.
